questions.question: According to the Census of India 2011, what is the percentage of India's population that live in urban areas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __31.16__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The total urban population in the country as per Census 2011 is more than 377 million** forming 31.16% of the total population.**
 
• The data shows that Goa is the most **urbanized state with 62.17% of the population living in urban areas**. But if one goes by geographical area and total population, Tamil Nadu is the most urbanized state followed by Kerala (47.7 percent) upstaging Maharashtra (45.2 percent)
 
• The total rural population in the country as per the census of 2011 is 833.1 million. 
 
 
• Himachal Pradesh becomes the most rural state with **89.97 percent of the rural population followed by Bihar.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The responsibility of conducting the decennial Census rests with the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.
 
• Census of India 2011 is the 15th census conducted in India, which is the largest democratic country in the world.
 
• The census data is collected every 10 years, and it provides important information about the population, literacy rate, occupation, and other demographic factors.
 
• The percentage of India's population that lives in urban areas has been increasing over the years due to various factors such as urbanization, industrialization, and modernization.
 
• According to the 2011 census, the percentage of India's population living in urban areas is 31.16% which is a significant increase from the previous census in 2001.
 
• Urbanization has both positive and negative impacts on society, and it is important to manage it effectively to ensure sustainable development.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution directs the state to provide for a 'Uniform Civil Code'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 44.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 44 of the Directive Principles in the Constitution says:**

 
 
• "State shall endeavor to provide for its citizens a uniform civil code (UCC) throughout the territory of India".
 
 
 
• The objective of Article 44 of the Directive Principles in the Indian Constitution was to address the discrimination against vulnerable groups and harmonize diverse cultural groups across the country.
 
• The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) calls for the formulation of one law for India, which would be applicable to all religious communities in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption.
 
• The origin of the UCC dates back to colonial India when the British government submitted its report in 1835 stressing the need for uniformity in the codification of Indian law relating to crimes, evidence, and contracts, specifically recommending that personal laws of Hindus and Muslims be kept outside such codification.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 43 **of the Indian Constitution directs the state to secure for all workers a** living wage, decent working conditions, and social security. **
 
• **Article 45** of the Indian Constitution directs the state to provide free and compulsory education for all **children between the ages of 6 and 14 years. **
 
• **Article 42 **of the Indian Constitution directs the state to make provisions for **securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.**

questions.question: Which experiment was designed to trace the motion of the earth through the 'luminiferous aether', a theoretical substance necessary for the transmission of light?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the __**Michelson and Morley experiment.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Michelson and Morley experiment was designed to trace the earth's motion through the luminiferous aether, a theoretical substance necessary for transmitting light.**
 
• The experiment was conducted in **1887 by Albert Michelson and Edward Morley.**
 
• The experiment aimed to detect the relative motion of the earth and the luminiferous aether by measuring the speed of light in different directions.
 
• The experiment results were surprising as they showed that the speed of light was constant in all directions, which contradicted the prevailing theory of the existence of the luminiferous aether.
 
• The Michelson and Morley experiment paved the way for the development of Einstein's theory of relativity, which explained the behavior of light and the absence of the luminiferous aether.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Maxwell and Hertz experiment: **This experiment was conducted by James Clerk Maxwell and Heinrich Hertz in the late 19th century to demonstrate the existence of electromagnetic waves.
 
• **Faraday and Henry experiment:** This experiment was conducted by Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry in the 19th century to study the phenomenon of electromagnetic induction.
 
• **Marconi and Thomson experiment: **This experiment was conducted by Guglielmo Marconi and Joseph John Thomson in the early 20th century to demonstrate the feasibility of wireless communication.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT one of the reasons for the break in the five year plans after three consequent five year plans were formulated?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the__** Gulf War.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• India's government formulated five-year plans to set targets for economic growth and development over five years.
 
• The first five-year plan was launched in 1951, and subsequent procedures were formulated until the 12th five-year plan ended in 2017.
 
• ** The break in five-year plans occurred after three consequent plans were formulated - the 7th, 8th, and 9th five-year plans.**
 
• The reasons for the break were primarily domestic issues such as the **Indo-Pakistan conflict, the devaluation of domestic currency, and two successive years of drought.**
 
• The Gulf War, which took place in 1990-91, impacted the global economy but was not a direct cause of the break in five-year plans in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

Five-Year Plans:

__
 
• The idea of a five-year plan is simple- The Government of India prepares a document with all its income and expenditure for five years.
 
• The budget of the central government and all the state governments is divided into two parts: non-plan and plan budgets.
 
• The non-plan budget is spent on routine items yearly. The planned budget is spent on a five-year basis as per the priorities fixed by the plan.
 
• The model of the Indian economy was premised on the concept of planning based on** five-year plans from 1951 to 2017.**
 
• The Five Year Plans were formulated, implemented, and regulated by a body known as the Planning Commission.

 
 

 Plan
 Aim/Goal
 
 

 First
 economic development
 
 

 Second
 rapid industrialization and the public sector
 
 

 Third
 agriculture development and growth
 
 

 Fourth
 Growth, Stability, and self-reliance.
 
 

 Fifth
 employment and poverty alleviation
 
 

 Sixth
 economic liberation 
 
 

 Seventh
 Industrial productivity levels through the use of technology
 
 

 Eighth
 modernisation of Industries
 
 

 Ninth
 elimination of poverty 
 
 

 Tenth
 inclusive growth and equitable development
 
 

 Eleventh
 rapid and more inclusive growth
 
 

 Twelfth
 Faster, More Inclusive, and Sustainable Growth
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**** 

Indo-Pakistan conflict:**

__
 
• The Indo-Pakistan conflict refers to the tensions and conflicts between India and Pakistan, primarily over the disputed region of Kashmir.
 
• The conflict has had an impact on India's economy and has been a factor in the break-in of five-year plans due to the diversion of resources towards defense and security.

**Devaluation of domestic currency:**

 
• Devaluation of domestic currency refers to reducing the currency's value relative to other currencies.
 
• This can lead to inflation and other economic problems, which can impact the targets set in the five-year plans.
 
• The devaluation of the Indian rupee in the 1990s was a factor in the break-in five-year plans.

**Two successive years of drought:**__

 
• Droughts can have a significant impact on agriculture, which is a major sector of the Indian economy.
 
• Two successive years of drought can lead to food shortages, inflation, and other economic problems, which can impact the targets set in the five-year plans.
 
• The droughts in the mid-1960s were a factor in the break in five-year plans.

questions.question: Who founded the East India Association in London?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __London__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji founded The East India Association in 1866.**
 
• He founded it with Indian members and retired British officials in London.
 
• It was supplanted by the London Indian Society.
 
• The objective behind the association was:
 
 
• to provide a platform for discussing matters and ideas about India,
 
• and to provide representation for Indians to the Government.
 
 
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji delivered the first lecture at the Association on 2 May 1867.
 
• The first President of the East India Association was Lord Lyveden.
 
• The East India Association incorporated the National Indian Association in 1949 and became the Britain, India, and Pakistan Association.
 
• In 1966 it amalgamated with the former India Society, now Royal India, Pakistan, and Ceylon Society, to become the Royal Society for India, Pakistan, and Ceylon.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ananda Mohan Bose was a prominent Bengali nationalist **and one of the founders of the Indian National Congress, but he was not involved in the East India Association.

 
 
• ​In 1872, Anand Mohan Bose formed an Indian Society in London to foster the spirit of nationalism among the Indian residents in Britain.
 
 
 
• AO Hume was a British civil servant who played a crucial role in forming the Indian National Congress, but he was not associated with the East India Association.
 
• Justice Ranade was a prominent social reformer and nationalist from Maharashtra, but he did not have any connection with the East India Association.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The London Indian Society
 
 
• ​In 1865, the London Indian Society was founded under the guidance of Dadabhai Naoroji.
 
• It was formed by Indian students as a forum to air political grievances.
 
• Europeans were allowed to be honorary members but could not vote or hold office.
 
• Of the founding group of students, they included W. C. Bonnerjee, Manomohun Ghose, Pherozeshah Mehta and Badruddin Tyabji.
 
• In 1866, the London Indian Society was superseded by the East India Association, although it did continue to exist in some separate form for a few more years.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor impacting India's climate?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the __** Sahara Desert.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Himalayan Mountains play a significant role i**n India's climate, as they act as a barrier to **cold winds from Central Asia** and help regulate the temperature in the northern part of the country.
 
• **The Indian Ocean **is another important factor, as it moderates the climate along the** coast and influences the monsoon season,** which is critical for agriculture and water supply in India.
 
• **The Western Ghats**, a mountain range along the western coast of India, also have a** significant impact on the climate,** as they block the southwest monsoon winds and cause heavy rainfall in the region.
 
• **However, the Sahara Desert, which is located in North Africa, is too far away from India to have any direct impact on its climate. It may indirectly affect the climate in some parts of the world through atmospheric circulation patterns, but not in India.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Himalayan Mountains **are a range of high peaks that stretch across several countries, including **India, Nepal, Bhutan, and China.**

 
 
• They are home to several glaciers and rivers that are critical for water supply in the region.
 
 
 
• The Sahara Desert is the world's largest hot desert, covering about 3.6 million square miles.
 
 
• It is known for its extreme temperatures and low rainfall and is home to several unique species of plants and animals that have adapted to the harsh conditions.
 
 
 
• **The Indian Ocean is the third largest ocean** in the world, covering an area of about 70 million square miles.
 
 
• It is home to several important shipping routes and is known for its rich biodiversity, including several species of whales, dolphins, and sea turtles.
 
 
 
• **The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site** known for their rich biodiversity, including several endemic species of plants and animals.
 
 
• They are also home to several tribal communities that have lived in the region for centuries.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

**FACTORS DETERMINING THE CLIMATE OF INDIA**

**Latitude :**

 
• The northern part of India lies in the sub-tropical and temperate zone and the part lying south of the Tropic of Cancer falls in the tropical zone.
 
• The tropical zone being nearer to the equator experiences high temperatures throughout the year with small daily and annual ranges.
 
• The area north of the Tropic of Cancer away from the equator experiences an extreme climate with a high daily and annual range of temperature.

**The Himalayan Mountains :**

 
• The lofty Himalayas in the north along with its extensions act as an effective climatic divide.
 
• The towering mountain chain provides an invincible shield to protect the subcontinent from the cold northern winds.
 
• These cold and chilly winds originate near the Arctic Circle and blow across central and eastern Asia.
 
• The Himalayas also trap the monsoon winds, forcing them to shed their moisture within the subcontinent.

**Distribution of Land and Water :**

 
• India is flanked by the Indian Ocean on three sides in the south and girdled by a high and continuous mountain wall in the north. As compared to the landmass, water heats up or cools down slowly.
 
• This differential heating of land and sea creates different air pressure zones in different seasons in and around the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Difference in air pressure causes a reversal in the direction of monsoon winds.

**Distance from the Sea :**

 
• With a long coastline, large coastal areas have an equable climate. Areas in the interior of India are far away from the moderating influence of the sea. Such areas have extremes of climate.
 
• That is why, the people of Mumbai and the Konkan coast have hardly any idea of extremes of temperature and the seasonal rhythm of weather.
 
• On the other hand, the seasonal contrasts in weather at places in the interior of the country such as Delhi, Kanpur and Amritsar affect the entire sphere of life.

**Altitude :**

 
• Temperature decreases with height. Due to thin air, places in the mountains are cooler than places on the plains.
 
• For example, Agra and Darjeeling are located on the same latitude, but the temperature of January in Agra is 16°C whereas it is only 4°C in Darjeeling.

**Relief :**

 
• The physiography or relief of India also affects the temperature, air pressure, direction and speed of wind and the amount and distribution of rainfall.
 
• The windward sides of Western Ghats and Assam receive high rainfall during June-September whereas the southern plateau remains dry due to its leeward situation along the Western Ghats.

questions.question:
Calculate the NNP (in ₹ crore) at market price from the given data.

 
 

 **Particulars**
 **Value (in ₹ crore)**
 
 

 NDP at factor cost
 1,25,250
 
 

 Net income from aboard
 (-) 581
 
 

 Net indirect taxes
 18,120
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1,42,789**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• To calculate the Net National Product (NNP) at market prices, we can use the following formula:
 
 
• **NNP at market prices = NDP at factor cost + Net Indirect Taxes + Net Income from Abroad**
 
 
 
• Given the data:
 
 
• NDP at factor cost: ₹1,25,250 crore
 
• Net Indirect Taxes: ₹18,120 crore
 
• Net Income from Abroad: -₹581 crore (negative value indicating net outflow)
 
 
 
• Now, substituting these values into the formula:
 
 
• NNP at market prices=1,25,250+18,120−581 NNP at market prices=1,25,250+18,120−581 NNP at market prices=1,25,250+18,120−581
 
• NNP at market prices=1,25,250+18,120−581=1,42,789 crore
 
• Therefore, the NNP at market prices is ₹1,42,789 crore.
 
 
 
• NDP at factor cost is the total value of goods and services produced within the domestic territory of a country in a financial year.
 
• It is calculated by deducting depreciation from GDP (Gross Domestic Product) at factor cost.
 
• Net income from abroad represents the income earned by domestic residents from foreign sources minus the income earned by foreign residents from domestic sources.
 
• Net indirect taxes refer to the indirect taxes paid by the **government minus the subsidies received by the government.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__ **

 
• Market Price and Factor Cost represent two different ways to value the goods and services within an economy.
 
• **Market Price:**
 
 
• The market price is the amount that consumers pay for a good or service in the marketplace.
 
• It includes the cost of production as well as taxes (indirect taxes) levied on the product or service and any subsidies provided by the government.
 
• The market price represents the final price paid by consumers, which also covers the cost of making the product available in the market (transportation, retailing, etc.).
 
 
 
• **Factor Cost:**
 
 
• Factor cost is the total production cost of goods and services, measured as the sum of the income earned by the factors of production (land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship).
 
• In simple terms, it is the cost of employing resources in producing goods and services, without considering any taxes or subsidies.
 
• Factor cost provides a perspective on the costs acquired by businesses in an economy to produce the goods and services that are consumed.
 
 
 
• Using the concepts of market price and factor cost, we can differentiate between NNP at Market prices and NNP at Factor cost:
 
• **NNP (Net National Product) at Market Price:**
 
 
• This is the value of final goods and services produced within an economy, including net income from abroad, measured at market prices. It includes indirect taxes and excludes subsidies paid by the government.
 
• It is essentially the GDP (Gross Domestic Product) adjusted for depreciation and net factor income from abroad.
 
 
 
• **NNP at Factor Cost:**
 
 
• This is the value of final goods and services produced within the economy, including net income from abroad, measured at factor cost.
 
• To calculate NNP at factor cost, we deduct indirect taxes and add subsidies to the NNP at market price.
 
• This gives us a measure of the income generated by the factors of production, disregarding the taxes and subsidies that may affect the market price.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a political philosophy of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: Sensitive for the historically disadvantaged groups
Sensitive to the needs of religious and linguistic minorities
Non-committal to building a common national identity

questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** Non-committal to building a common national identity.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sensitive for the historically disadvantaged groups**

 
 
• The Indian Constitution recognizes the need to provide special provisions and safeguards for historically disadvantaged groups such as Dalits, Adivasis, and women.
 
• This is evident in the provisions for reservations in education and employment, as well as the creation of special laws such as the Prevention of Atrocities Act.
 
 
 
• **Open to community values**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution recognizes the importance of community values and traditions, but only to the extent that they do not violate fundamental rights and principles.
 
• This is evident in the provisions for freedom of religion and the protection of cultural and linguistic minorities.
 
 
 
• **Sensitive to the needs of religious and linguistic minorities**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution recognizes the importance of protecting the rights and interests of religious and linguistic minorities.
 
• This is evident in the provisions for freedom of religion, the right to language, and the creation of minority commissions.
 
 
 
• **Non-committal to building a common national identity**
 
 
• T**he Indian Constitution recognizes the importance of building a common national identity but does not prescribe a specific model or ideology.**
 
• **This is evident in the use of terms such as "unity in diversity" and the recognition of multiple languages and cultures**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**Characteristics of Indian Polity:**

 
• Separation of Power:
 
 
• The theory of Separation of Power was first published by Montesquieu in his book "Espirit des Louis’ (The Spirit of the laws)" in 1747.
 
• This principle enables the three pillars of democracy - executive, judiciary, and legislature to perform separate functions and act as separate entities.
 
• It is a part of the basic structure of the Indian Constitution.
 
• ​In Raj Narain v/s The State of Uttar Pradesh case, 1975 the Supreme Court clarified that India has separation of power in the broad sense only.
 
 
 
• ​Checks and Balances:
 
 
• ​This principle enables the three pillars of democracy - executive, judiciary, and legislature to support and prevent each other's arbitrary decision-making.
 
• **Article 75 implies that the executive is responsible to the legislature for his decisions.**
 
• The judiciary checks the legislature through the power of judicial review.
 
• Appointment of judges in India is done through the President.
 
 
 
• Parliamentary System:
 
 
• In India, it is inspired by the UK's Westminster model.
 
• In this system, the de facto head is the Prime Minister while the de jure head is the President or Monarch.
 
• Ivor Jennings called the parliamentary system a ‘cabinet system’ because the cabinet is the nucleus of power in a parliamentary system.
 
 
 
• Limited Government:
 
 
• ​This is also known as Constitutionalism because the powers to legislate are limited by the Constitution itself.
 
• It prevents arbitrary decision-making.
 
• Unlike the UK, India has a limited government.

questions.question:
Which of the following is true?

A) Fiscal deficit is financed from borrowings.

B) Recovery of loans is a revenue receipt.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** Only A.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** Fiscal deficit refers to the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total revenue.**

 
 
• **It is financed through borrowings, either from domestic or foreign sources.**
 
 
 
• ** Recovery of loans is not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. **
 
 
• Revenue receipts are those that **do not create any liability or reduce any asset of the government, **such as** taxes, fines, and fees. Capital receipts, on the other hand,** are those that create a liability or reduce an asset of the government, such as borrowings, disinvestment proceeds, and recoveries of loans. 
 
 
 
• In summary, the** fiscal deficit is financed from borrowings **and the **recovery of loans is a capital receipt** .
 
• It is worth noting tha**t fiscal deficit is a key indicator of a government's financial health** and economic management.
 
• A high fiscal deficit may lead to i**nflation, high interest rates, and a negative impact** on the country's credit rating.
 
• Therefore, governments often strive to maintain a **low fiscal deficit through various **measures such as reducing expenditure, increasing revenue, and improving tax compliance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• What constitutes the government’s total income or receipts?
 
 
• It has two components revenue receipts and non-tax revenues.
 
 
• Revenue receipts from the government
 
 
• Corporation Tax
 
• Income Tax
 
• Custom Duties
 
• Union Excise Duties
 
• GST and taxes of Union territories.
 
 
 
• Non-tax revenues
 
 
• Interest Receipts
 
• Dividends and Profits
 
• External Grants
 
• Other non-tax revenues
 
• Receipts of union territories
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• Expenditures of the government:
 
 
• Revenue Expenditure
 
• Capital Expenditure
 
• Interest Payments
 
• Grants-in-aid for the creation of capital assets.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fiscal Deficit is the difference between the total income of the government (total taxes and non-debt capital receipts) and its total expenditure.** While calculating the total revenue, borrowings are not included. Hence, Fiscal Deficit is- Budget expenditure- Budget receipts excluding borrowings.

 
 
• A fiscal deficit situation occurs when the government’s expenditure exceeds its income. This difference is calculated both in absolute terms and also as a percentage of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of the country. A recurring high fiscal deficit means that the government has been spending beyond its means.
 
• The government describes fiscal deficit of India as “the excess of total disbursements from the Consolidated Fund of India, excluding repayment of the debt, over total receipts into the Fund (excluding the debt receipts) during a financial year”.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct expression?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __Net investment = Gross investment - depreciation__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The addition to the capital stock in an economy is measured by net investment or new capital formation, which is expressed as
 
 
• **Net investment = Gross investment - depreciation.**
 
 
 
• **Gross Investment is referred to as the total expenditure that is made for buying capital goods over a time period**, without accounting for depreciation.
 
 
• In other words, gross investment is the amount that a company has invested in particular assets or the business as a whole without considering depreciation for the same.
 
 
 
• Net Investment, on the other hand, is the actual addition that is made to the capital stock in a given period.
 
 
• Net Investment takes into account the depreciation and is calculated by subtracting the depreciation from the gross investment.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) refers to the market value of all final goods and services produced within an economy.

 
• It can be calculated into two ways:
 
 
• Nominal GDP:
 
 
• It refers to the GDP at the current market prices i.e., the GDP is calculated as per the market prices for the year for which the GDP is calculated.
 
 
 
• Real GDP:
 
 
• It refers to the GDP at base year prices i.e., the GDP is calculated as per the market prices in the base year. Thus, the Real GDP negates the inflation in goods and services.
 
 
 
• In case of a high rate of inflation, the nominal GDP would be higher than the real GDP.

questions.question: 'Ghiyasuddin Balban introduced the customs of 'Sijda' and 'Paibos' as normal forms of salutations to the king as a part of ______ etiquette.
questions.solution:

__
 
• **The customs of 'Sijda' and 'Paibos' were introduced by Ghiyasuddin Balban as normal forms of salutations to the king as a part of Court etiquette.**
 
• ** 'Sijda' **is a form of **prostration **where an** individual bows down to the ground** and* touches their forehead to the floor as a sign of respect,* submission, and humility.

• **Ghiyasuddin Balban (1266-1287)**

 
 
• He was the first Sultan of Delhi to introduce the practice of 'Sijda'.
 
• He started Sijda (prostration) and Paibos as the normal form of Salutation of the king.
 
• In Sijda people had to Kneel down and touch the ground with their heads to greet the Sultan.
